Authority. The recognized right of an individual or institution to make decisions, issue commands, and expect compliance from others. Authority arises from social recognition, legal structures, or traditions that grant certain actors legitimacy in governing behavior. It is central to understanding how societies organize power and maintain order.

Authority is distinguished from raw power because it implies consent or acceptance by those being governed, even if that consent is coerced or implicit. Legitimate authority derives its force from shared norms, law, tradition, or expertise, while illegitimate authority governs through fear or deception alone.

Psychological research has illuminated how authority shapes behavior. Milgram's obedience studies demonstrated that ordinary people will comply with authority figures even when asked to inflict harm. The Stanford Prison Experiment showed how situational authority—the assignment of guard and prisoner roles—can rapidly reshape behavior and social dynamics. Authority structures exist in families, schools, workplaces, militaries, and governments, embedded in hierarchy and formal roles.

Anthropologist Bronislaw Malinowski observed that all functional societies vest authority in chieftains, elders, or councils to coordinate collective action. Authority requires no violence, just submission to someone perceived as having the right to command. It differs from influence—you may be influenced by a peer's suggestion, but authority is obeyed because disobeying feels transgressive or dangerous.

In organizations, authority can be de jure, formal and codified in law or rules, or de facto, exercised informally by those with practical power. Challenge to authority often precedes social change—revolutions, civil rights movements, and reformations all hinge on questioning established legitimacy.
